## Why Go Beyond Plain SQL?

```{=html}
<p>SQL is <b>declarative</b>: you describe <i>what</i> result you want. Some tasks need step-by-step logic: loops, conditions, variables and reusable routines. SQL:1999 added <b>functions</b>, <b>procedures</b> and <b>procedural constructs</b>, and <b>triggers</b> run code automatically when data changes.</p>
<div class="flow tight"><div class="box"><b>Functions</b><span>return a value or a table</span></div><div class="box"><b>Procedures</b><span>called with call, out parameters</span></div><div class="box"><b>Constructs</b><span>variables, loops, if, case, exceptions</span></div><div class="box"><b>Triggers</b><span>run automatically on insert / update / delete</span></div></div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Lecture syntax vs PostgreSQL</div><p style="margin:0 0 6px">The lectures use SQL-standard syntax (SQL/PSM). PostgreSQL implements the same ideas in its procedural language <b>PL/pgSQL</b>, with a different syntax. Each section below shows the lecture version first, then the version that runs in PostgreSQL.</p><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>Idea</th><th>Lecture (SQL standard)</th><th>PostgreSQL (PL/pgSQL)</th></tr><tr><td>function body</td><td><code>begin … end</code></td><td><code>as $$ … $$ language plpgsql;</code></td></tr><tr><td>local variables</td><td><code>declare</code> inside <code>begin</code></td><td><code>declare</code> before <code>begin</code></td></tr><tr><td>table function</td><td><code>return table (select …)</code></td><td><code>returns table (…)</code> + <code>select</code> body</td></tr><tr><td>using a table function</td><td><code>select * from table(f(…))</code></td><td><code>select * from f(…)</code></td></tr><tr><td>loops</td><td><code>while … do … end while</code>, <code>repeat … until … end repeat</code></td><td><code>while … loop … end loop</code>, <code>loop … exit when … end loop</code></td></tr><tr><td>else-if</td><td><code>elseif</code></td><td><code>elsif</code></td></tr><tr><td>exceptions</td><td><code>declare … handler</code>, <code>signal</code></td><td><code>exception when …</code>, <code>raise exception</code></td></tr><tr><td>trigger body</td><td>written inside <code>create trigger</code></td><td>a separate trigger function, then <code>create trigger … execute function</code></td></tr><tr><td>new / old row</td><td><code>referencing new row as nrow</code></td><td>built-in <code>new</code> and <code>old</code></td></tr></table></div></div>
<p>All examples run on the <b>university</b> or <b>flis</b> dataset inside <code>begin; … rollback;</code>, so the functions, triggers and data changes disappear afterwards. Remove <code>begin</code>/<code>rollback</code> to keep them.</p>
```

## Functions

```{=html}
<p>A function takes parameters and returns a value, so it can be used inside a query like a built-in function. <i>Example:</i> the number of instructors in a department.</p><div class="flow-label">Lecture syntax</div>
```

```sql
create function dept_count(dept_name varchar(20))
returns integer
begin
    declare d_count integer;
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = dept_name;
    return d_count;
end
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div><div class="ds">Dataset: university</div>
```

```sql
create function dept_count(d_name varchar(20))
returns integer as $$
declare
    d_count integer;
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
    return d_count;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;
```

```{=html}
<p>The parameter is named <code>d_name</code> rather than <code>dept_name</code>: in PostgreSQL, a parameter with the same name as a column makes <code>dept_name</code> ambiguous inside the query.</p>
```

```sql
select dept_count('Physics');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_count</th></tr><tr><td>2</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
```

```sql
-- departments with more than 4 instructors
select dept_name, budget
from department
where dept_count(dept_name) > 4;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_name</th><th>budget</th></tr><tr><td>Athletics</td><td>734550.70</td></tr><tr><td>Statistics</td><td>395051.74</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(2 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">What happens</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>for each department</b></div><span>outer row</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>call dept_count</b></div><span>counts its instructors</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>&gt; 4?</b></div><span>keep the row</span></div></div></div>
<p>A function whose body is a single query can also be written in plain SQL:</p>
```

```sql
create function dept_count_sql(d_name varchar(20))
returns bigint as $$
    select count(*) from instructor where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
$$ language sql;

select dept_count_sql('Statistics');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_count_sql</th></tr><tr><td>6</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
```

### Table Functions

```{=html}
<p>A <b>table function</b> returns a relation and is used in the <code>from</code> clause, like a parameterised view.</p><div class="flow-label">Lecture syntax</div>
```

```sql
create function instructor_of(dept_name varchar(20))
returns table (id varchar(5), name varchar(20),
               dept_name varchar(20), salary numeric(8,2))
return table
    (select id, name, dept_name, salary
     from instructor
     where instructor.dept_name = instructor_of.dept_name);

select * from table(instructor_of('Music'));
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div>
```

```sql
create function instructor_of(d_name varchar(20))
returns table (id varchar(5), name varchar(20),
               dept_name varchar(20), salary numeric(8,2)) as $$
    select id, name, dept_name, salary
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
$$ language sql;

select * from instructor_of('Biology');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>id</th><th>name</th><th>dept_name</th><th>salary</th></tr><tr><td>80759</td><td>Queiroz</td><td>Biology</td><td>45538.32</td></tr><tr><td>81991</td><td>Valtchev</td><td>Biology</td><td>77036.18</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(2 rows)</div>
<p>⚠️ The lecture form <code>select * from table(instructor_of('Biology'))</code> gives <code>syntax error at or near "table"</code> in PostgreSQL. Call the function directly in <code>from</code>.</p>
```

### Procedures

```{=html}
<p>A <b>procedure</b> is invoked with <code>call</code> and returns results through <code>out</code> parameters instead of a return value.</p><div class="flow-label">Lecture syntax</div>
```

```sql
create procedure dept_count_proc(in dept_name varchar(20),
                                 out d_count integer)
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = dept_count_proc.dept_name;
end

declare d_count integer;
call dept_count_proc('Physics', d_count);
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div>
```

```sql
create procedure dept_count_proc(in d_name varchar(20),
                                 out d_count integer) as $$
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

call dept_count_proc('Physics', null);   -- pass null for the out parameter
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>d_count</th></tr><tr><td>2</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th></th><th>Function</th><th>Procedure</th></tr><tr><td>Invoked by</td><td>used inside a query</td><td><code>call</code> statement</td></tr><tr><td>Returns</td><td>a value or a table</td><td>values through <code>out</code> parameters</td></tr><tr><td>Overloading</td><td>allowed: same name, different parameter types</td><td>allowed: same name, different parameter types</td></tr></table></div>
```

## Procedural Language Constructs

### Variables, `for` loops and `if`

```{=html}
<p><i>Example:</i> compute league points for a team: 3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss. The <code>for</code> loop visits every match the team played.</p><div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div>
```

```sql
create function team_points(t_id varchar(5))
returns integer as $$
declare
    points integer := 0;
    m record;                                   -- holds one match row
begin
    for m in select * from matches
             where host_team_id = t_id or guest_team_id = t_id
    loop
        if m.host_team_score = m.guest_team_score then
            points := points + 1;                   -- draw
        elsif (m.host_team_id = t_id and m.host_team_score > m.guest_team_score)
           or (m.guest_team_id = t_id and m.guest_team_score > m.host_team_score) then
            points := points + 3;                   -- win
        end if;                                     -- loss: no points
    end loop;
    return points;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select name, team_points(team_id) as points
from teams
order by points desc, name;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>points</th></tr><tr><td>Black Eagles</td><td>13</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>8</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>5</td></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>4</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(6 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">One loop iteration</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>fetch next match</b></div><span>into m</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>draw?</b></div><span>+1</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>won as host or guest?</b></div><span>+3</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>otherwise</b></div><span>+0, next match</span></div></div></div>
```

### `while` loops

```{=html}
<p><i>Example:</i> how many years until a department's budget reaches 1,000,000 if it grows by 5% a year?</p><div class="ds">Dataset: university</div>
```

```sql
create function years_to_reach(d_name varchar(20), target numeric)
returns integer as $$
declare
    b numeric;
    years integer := 0;
begin
    select budget into b from department where dept_name = d_name;
    while b < target loop
        b := b * 1.05;
        years := years + 1;
    end loop;
    return years;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select dept_name, budget, years_to_reach(dept_name, 1000000) as years
from department
where dept_name in ('Physics', 'Biology', 'Math');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_name</th><th>budget</th><th>years</th></tr><tr><td>Biology</td><td>647610.55</td><td>9</td></tr><tr><td>Physics</td><td>942162.76</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Math</td><td>777605.11</td><td>6</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(3 rows) · row order may vary</div>
<p>The lecture's <code>repeat … until … end repeat</code> (body runs at least once) is written in PL/pgSQL as <code>loop … exit when &lt;condition&gt;; end loop;</code>.</p>
```

### `case`

```{=html}
<p>A <code>case</code> <b>expression</b> works in any query; PL/pgSQL also has a <code>case</code> <b>statement</b> with the same shape, ending in <code>end case</code>.</p><div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div>
```

```sql
select name, team_points(team_id) as points,
       case
           when team_points(team_id) >= 9 then 'Top'
           when team_points(team_id) >= 5 then 'Middle'
           else 'Bottom'
       end as band
from teams
order by points desc;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>points</th><th>band</th></tr><tr><td>Black Eagles</td><td>13</td><td>Top</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>8</td><td>Middle</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>7</td><td>Middle</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>7</td><td>Middle</td></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>5</td><td>Middle</td></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>4</td><td>Bottom</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(6 rows) · order of the two 7-point teams may vary</div>
```

### Exception Handling

```{=html}
<div class="flow-label">Lecture syntax</div>
```

```sql
declare out_of_classroom_seats condition
declare exit handler for out_of_classroom_seats
begin
    ...
end
-- the handler runs when the condition is raised with:
signal out_of_classroom_seats
```

```{=html}
<p>In PL/pgSQL, an <code>exception</code> section at the end of a block catches errors raised inside it. <i>Example:</i> add an instructor, returning a friendly message instead of an error.</p><div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div><div class="ds">Dataset: university</div>
```

```sql
create function add_instructor(i_id varchar(5), i_name varchar(20),
                               d_name varchar(20), sal numeric)
returns text as $$
begin
    insert into instructor values (i_id, i_name, d_name, sal);
    return 'added ' || i_name;
exception
    when unique_violation      then return 'id ' || i_id || ' already exists';
    when check_violation       then return 'salary must be above 29000';
    when foreign_key_violation then return 'no department called ' || d_name;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;
```

```{=html}
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Four calls, four outcomes</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>call</th><th>constraint hit</th><th>returns</th></tr><tr class="hit"><td>add_instructor('30765', 'Green', 'Biology', 72000)</td><td>none</td><td>added Green</td></tr><tr><td>add_instructor('63395', 'Copy', 'Biology', 72000)</td><td>primary key</td><td>id 63395 already exists</td></tr><tr><td>add_instructor('30766', 'Low', 'Biology', 20000)</td><td>check (salary &gt; 29000)</td><td>salary must be above 29000</td></tr><tr><td>add_instructor('30767', 'Lee', 'Music', 50000)</td><td>foreign key</td><td>no department called Music</td></tr></table></div></div>
<p>To raise your own error (the lecture's <code>signal</code>), use <code>raise exception</code>:</p>
```

```sql
create function check_budget(d_name varchar(20))
returns numeric as $$
declare
    b numeric;
begin
    select budget into b from department where dept_name = d_name;
    if b is null then
        raise exception 'department % not found', d_name;
    end if;
    return b;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select check_budget('Physics');
select check_budget('Music');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><pre> check_budget
--------------
    942162.76

ERROR:  department Music not found</pre>
```

### External Language Routines

```{=html}
<p>Functions can also be written in languages such as C, Java or Python (PostgreSQL: <code>language plpython3u</code>, <code>language c</code>). They can be faster and more expressive, but code running inside the database server can crash it or access data it should not. Safer options run the code in a sandbox (Java, Python) or in a separate process, at some performance cost.</p>
```

## Triggers

```{=html}
<p>A <b>trigger</b> is a statement the system executes automatically when a specified change is made to the database. It follows the <b>event–condition–action</b> model:</p>
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>Event</b></div><span>insert, update or delete on a relation</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>Condition</b></div><span>optional when (…)</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>Action</b></div><span>the code to run</span></div></div>
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>Choice</th><th>Options</th></tr><tr><td>Timing</td><td><b>before</b> the change (validate or modify the new row) · <b>after</b> the change (update other tables, log)</td></tr><tr><td>Granularity</td><td><b>for each row</b>: once per affected row, with <code>old</code> / <code>new</code> · <b>for each statement</b>: once per statement, with transition tables of all old / new rows</td></tr></table></div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">When does each trigger run?</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box grey"><b>Event</b></div><span>insert / update / delete issued</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>BEFORE trigger</b></div><span>validate or modify the new row first</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box grey"><b>Database operation</b></div><span>row is written to the table</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>AFTER trigger</b></div><span>update other tables, audit, alert</span></div></div><p style="margin:6px 0 0">A BEFORE trigger can change <code>new</code> or cancel the change (by returning <code>null</code>); by the time an AFTER trigger runs, the row is already stored.</p></div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Row-level vs statement-level: <code>update instructor … where dept_name = 'Physics'</code> changes 2 rows</div><div class="two"><div><div class="flow-label">for each row</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>row 1</b></div><span>trigger fires</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>row 2</b></div><span>trigger fires</span></div></div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;text-align:center">fires <b>2 times</b>, sees <code>old</code> / <code>new</code></p></div><div><div class="flow-label">for each statement</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>rows 1 and 2</b></div><span>trigger fires once</span></div></div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;text-align:center">fires <b>once</b>, sees all rows via transition tables</p></div></div></div>
<p>In PostgreSQL, a trigger has two parts: a <b>trigger function</b> (<code>returns trigger</code>) that contains the action, and the <code>create trigger</code> statement that attaches it to a table.</p>
```

### BEFORE row trigger: clean up a value

```{=html}
<p>Convert a blank grade to <code>null</code> before it is stored.</p><div class="flow-label">Lecture syntax</div>
```

```sql
create trigger setnull_trigger before update on takes
referencing new row as nrow
for each row
when (nrow.grade = ' ')
begin atomic
    set nrow.grade = null;
end;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><pre>ERROR:  syntax error at or near "referencing"</pre><div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div><div class="ds">Dataset: university</div>
```

```sql
create function setnull_grade() returns trigger as $$
begin
    if new.grade = ' ' then
        new.grade := null;
    end if;
    return new;          -- the (possibly modified) row that gets stored
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger setnull_trigger
before update on takes
for each row
execute function setnull_grade();

update takes set grade = ' ' where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';
select id, course_id, grade from takes where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>id</th><th>course_id</th><th>grade</th></tr><tr><td>1000</td><td>642</td><td><span class="nl">null</span></td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
```

### AFTER row trigger: keep another table in sync

```{=html}
<p>When a failing or missing grade becomes a pass, add the course credits to the student's <code>tot_cred</code>.</p><div class="flow-label">PostgreSQL</div>
```

```sql
create function credits_earned() returns trigger as $$
begin
    update student
    set tot_cred = tot_cred +
        (select credits from course where course.course_id = new.course_id)
    where student.id = new.id;
    return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger credits_earned
after update of grade on takes
for each row
when (new.grade <> 'F' and new.grade is not null
      and (old.grade = 'F' or old.grade is null))
execute function credits_earned();
```

```{=html}
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Student 1000 (Manber), course 642 (3 credits)</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>update</th><th>old.grade → new.grade</th><th>when (…) true?</th><th>tot_cred</th></tr><tr><td>(start)</td><td>—</td><td>—</td><td>39</td></tr><tr><td>set grade = 'F'</td><td>C- → F</td><td>✗ new grade is F</td><td>39</td></tr><tr class="hit"><td>set grade = 'B'</td><td>F → B</td><td>✓ fail became pass</td><td><b>42</b></td></tr><tr><td>set grade = 'A'</td><td>B → A</td><td>✗ old grade was a pass</td><td>42</td></tr></table></div></div>
```

### Statement-level trigger

```{=html}
<p>Runs once per <code>update</code> statement, however many rows it touches. The transition tables hold all old and new rows. <i>Example:</i> log every salary update.</p>
```

```sql
create table salary_audit (changed_at timestamp default now(),
                           rows_changed integer,
                           total_increase numeric);

create function log_raise() returns trigger as $$
begin
    insert into salary_audit(rows_changed, total_increase)
    select count(*), sum(n.salary - o.salary)
    from new_rows n join old_rows o on n.id = o.id;
    return null;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger log_raise
after update on instructor
referencing old table as old_rows new table as new_rows
for each statement
execute function log_raise();

update instructor set salary = salary * 1.05 where dept_name = 'Physics';
select rows_changed, round(total_increase, 2) as total_increase from salary_audit;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>rows_changed</th><th>total_increase</th></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>11457.69</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row) · one audit row for the whole statement</div>
```

## Using Triggers Wisely

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>Good uses</th><th>Risks</th></tr><tr><td>Logging changes to an audit table</td><td>Too many triggers make it hard to see why data changed</td></tr><tr><td>Simple validation or clean-up of new rows</td><td>Business logic hidden where developers do not look</td></tr><tr><td>Keeping derived values in sync (like tot_cred)</td><td>A trigger can fire another trigger, causing chains of updates</td></tr><tr><td>Recording who changed what and when</td><td>Row-by-row work on large updates is slow</td></tr></table></div><p>Do not use triggers for things the system already does better: maintaining materialized views (use <code>refresh</code>) or replicating databases (use built-in replication). Disable triggers when loading data from a backup, or they will fire again on rows that were already processed.</p>
```
